newsitem.title: USA: Republican money advantage helped keep Congress.
newsitem.headline: Republican money advantage helped keep Congress.

text.p: Republicans built a large advantage over Democrats in political fundraising last year, with a big edge in private and corporate donations, according to two reports released on Friday.

Figures from the Federal Election Commmission (FEC) showed Republican Party committees raised nearly $549 million between Jan. 1 and Nov. 25, 1996. Democrats raised $332 million in the same period. Together this represented a 73 percent increase over the 1991-92 election cycle.

This money is divided into so-called "hard money" given to congressional candidates, which is subject to legal limits, and "soft money" which is not supposed to be used for elections and is not subject to control.

The Republicans raised $408 million in hard dollars against $210 million for the Democrats. In soft money, Republican Party committees raised $141 million, a 224 percent increase over 1992. Democrats raised $122 million, for a 237 percent increase.

Campaign finance reform has become a major issue facing the new Congress. It came to the forefront in the final weeks of last year's presidential campaign with disclosures that the Democratic Party raised large sums of money from wealthy Asian businessmen, and individuals who could not substantiate the true source of the money they provided.

The Democrats have returned over $1.5 million and face a Justice Department probe and the prospect of congressional hearings. President Bill Clinton is also under the microscope amid allegations that overseas interests donated huge sums of money to influence U.S. foreign policy.
A second, independent report issued on Friday argued that a large edge in corporate and private political donations helped the Republicans keep control of Congress in the elections.

The report by Citizen Action, a political watchdog group which monitors campaign fundraising, said the Republican advantage was concentrated in significant battleground races and proved decisive in allowing the party to maintain a narrow majority in the House of Representatives.
"This report confirms again what most Americans believe -- that more and more elections are determined by the highest bidder," said Citizen Action director Ira Arlook.
In recent days newspapers have reported that Republican leaders have put pressure on corporate interests to stop hedging their bets by giving money to both the Democrats and the Republicans.

The Citizen Action report said that where Democrats and Republicans enjoyed rough parity in their financial resources, Democrats tended to win. But when Republicans mustered a large money edge, they almost invariably won.
In the 10 closest House races won by Democrats, the Democratic candidates raised on average $94,000 less than their Republican opponents.
In 10 close races where Republicans won by two percent or less, they raised an average of $370,000 or 56 percent more than their opponents.
Corporate special interest political action committees contributed $97.8 million to Republican congressional candidates and $41.4 million to Democrats.
Large individual donors gave $197 million to Republican candidates, and $132 million to Democrats.
